newsitem.title: USA: House passes bill giving private workers comp time.
newsitem.headline: House passes bill giving private workers comp time.

text.p: The House Wednesday voted to let American workers take time off in lieu of overtime pay, a move Republicans called family friendly and President Clinton termed a threat to fair labour laws certain to draw a veto.

By a largely party-line vote of 222-210 lawmakers approved legislation amending a 1938 labour law that requires overtime pay for most employees who work more than 40 hours a week. Public sector employees already have the choice of choosing compensatory time instead of overtime cash.
Republican leaders and businesses have made the measure a priority, saying it would give hard-pressed working parents much needed flexibility to spend time with their families.

"The American family is stressed and strained in new ways each and every day ... too often in today's economy working parents are forced to choose between their families and their jobs," New Jersey Republican Representative Marge Roukema said.
Democrats and their union allies charged the bill undermined vital labour protections and would let businesses bully employees into working extra hours without extra pay.

"When real wages are stagnant or dropping for low- or middle-income Americans, the ability to work overtime is often the difference beween paying the rent and putting food on the table or being homeless and hungry," Representative Lucille Roybal-Allard, a California Democrat, said.
The Senate will take up a similar measure later this spring. Unless there is a breakthrough, the outlook is bleak.
In a letter to House Speaker Newt Gingrich, Clinton complained the legislation undermined labour laws and asked Republicans to work with him on a compromise.

"I intend to veto any legislation that fails to guarantee real choice for employees, real protection against employer abuse and preservation of fair labour standards such as the 40-hour work week," Clinton said.

The Working Families Flexibility Act would let private-sector businesses give their workers the choice of taking 1-1/2 hours of paid time off, called comp time, instead of time-and-a-half pay, for every hour of overtime worked. Any comp time agreement would have to be voluntary and workers would be able to withdraw from such arrangements. Accrued comp time not used would be cashed out each year.
Private employees who work for hourly wages, rather than professionals, are covered by the Fair Labour Standards Act requiring time-and-a-half pay after 40 hours of work a week.
About 57 percent of the work force, or 68 million employees, are hourly workers. Public sector employees already have the ability to opt for comp time.

Republicans angrily denied charges that workers would be subject to abuse under the bill, saying they had built in protections to ensure employers did not coerce employees into taking take comp time or punish any who wanted overtime.
Democrats said workers would have little say in using their comp time because the bill allows employers to deny requests for time off if they believed they would disrupt business.
They warned there was no real protection for workers who did not want to take comp time, leaving temporary and low-income workers especially vulnerable.
Clinton and Democrats instead want to expand the Family and Medical Leave law, which allows many workers to take unpaid time off.
